<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls and fractures are a major clinical concern for older adults. International clinical guidelines recommend annual fall risk screening for all adults aged 60 years and older. However, existing falls risk–screening algorithms have shown limited sensitivity and specificity in detecting future falls. Emerging health technologies, including wearable sensors, in-silico finite element models (FEMs), and virtual reality (VR) technology, show promise in enhancing fall and fracture risk assessments by providing more personalized objective data to support targeted primary prevention. However, large-scale longitudinal studies are required to evaluate their predictive accuracy and cost-effectiveness for systematic community–based screening.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The TARGET (Targeted Assessment and Recruitment of Geriatrics for Effective Fall Prevention Treatments) study is an ongoing national prospective cohort study in Singapore designed to develop cost-effective and scalable frameworks for the early detection and prevention of falls and fractures using novel health technologies. This paper describes the rationale, design, and baseline characteristics of TARGET, and provides preliminary insights into how these novel technologies perform in discriminating between older adults with and with no history of falls at study baseline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 2291 community-dwelling Singapore residents aged ≥60 years were enrolled between 2022 and 2024. Participants underwent a comprehensive baseline fall risk assessment comprising (1) home-based interview to assess sociodemographic, anthropometric, cognitive, physical, functional, and psychosocial status; (2) gait assessment using wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) motion sensors; (3) dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and whole-body 3D scans to construct subject-specific FEMs; and (4) VR-based cognitive assessment to probe spatial navigation deficits. Prospective follow-up for 2 years is ongoing, with linkage to national electronic medical records (EMRs) to obtain detailed clinical, medication, and pathological data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the total cohort, 58% (1327/2291) were female, with a mean age of 74.6 years at baseline. TARGET represents a relatively healthy older adult population, with 83% (1898/2291) remaining fully independent, 44% (1016/2290) with mild cognitive impairment, 50% (440/879) with osteopenia, and 15% (358/2291) reporting falls in the past year. Significant baseline functional, psychosocial, cognitive, and biomechanical differences were identified between fallers and nonfallers. Fallers had poorer physical and psychosocial health, greater gait variability, and a higher risk of osteoporotic fractures. Novel risk prediction models integrating epidemiological, IMUs, FEM, VR, and EMR data are in development and being validated against gold standard clinical assessments, with cost-effectiveness evaluations of the economic feasibility of adopting these screening measures at scale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leveraging comprehensive epidemiological, EMR, and health technology data, TARGET is well positioned to identify novel biomarkers and systemic interactions that may predict falls and fracture risk, with potential application to other age-related diseases with shared pathophysiology. In particular, TARGET’s focus on community-based screening using technologies that can be administered by nonclinical personnel has the potential to reduce substantial burden and costs within the health care sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Rationale, Design, and Baseline Characteristics of the TARGET (Targeted Assessment and Recruitment of Geriatrics for Effective Fall Prevention Treatments) Cohort of Older Adults for Assessing Fall and Fracture Risk: Prospective Cohort Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) lacks disease-modifying treatment, making early identification of modifiable risk factors in asymptomatic older adults a priority. Patellar tendon stiffness (PTS) and knee extensor strength (KESt) may independently influence KOA development, yet their prognostic value in individuals free of knee symptoms is unestablished.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to determine whether baseline extensor mechanism mechanical properties predict 2-year incident clinical KOA in community-dwelling older adults who were asymptomatic at enrollment, and to quantify the relative contribution of each parameter.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This 2-year prospective cohort study enrolled 116 community-dwelling older adults (220 knees) free of knee pain at baseline. Incident clinical KOA was diagnosed according to the American College of Rheumatology criteria. Prognostic performance was evaluated across 7 survival algorithms using 5-fold nested cross-validation with the Harrell C-index. Predictor importance was quantified using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) values from the best-performing model, and absolute KOA risk was estimated across tertiles of the linear predictor score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Over 2 years, 55 (25%) knees developed incident clinical KOA. PTS and KESt were consistently selected across all cross-validation folds, whereas quadriceps muscle passive stiffness was not selected in any fold. The gradient boosted survival model achieved the highest discrimination (C-index=0.720, 95% CI 0.686-0.754), significantly exceeding chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.05). SHAP analysis identified KESt as the dominant predictor (mean |SHAP| 0.314, 95% CI 0.251-0.388), with PTS as the second most important predictor (0.166, 95% CI 0.128-0.200). Knees in the highest-risk tertile showed a 24-month KOA incidence of 38.4% (28/73), which was more than twice that in the lowest-risk tertile (13/74, 17.6%).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PTS and KESt independently and consistently predicted 2-year incident clinical KOA in asymptomatic community-dwelling older adults. Extensor mechanism mechanical profiling may identify individuals at elevated KOA risk prior to symptom onset, although these exploratory findings require confirmation in larger cohorts before KESt and PTS can be considered for screening or preventive intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Prediction of 2-Year Incident Clinical Knee Osteoarthritis From Extensor Mechanism Mechanical Properties in Asymptomatic Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Prospective Cohort Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Smart home technologies (SHTs) hold promise for supporting aging in place, yet older adults’ technology adoption involves more than a straightforward response to perceived benefits. This study examined how privacy concerns and fear of dependency, along with other technology acceptance factors, are associated with behavioral intention to use SHTs, and whether these associations differ between older adults with and without prior SHT experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of 421 U.S. older adults aged 55 to 80. Drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, we assessed performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, along with privacy concerns and fear of dependency. Multiple regression analyses with interaction terms were estimated separately for experienced and inexperienced users, and pooled models with three-way interactions tested whether moderating associations differed by prior experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Performance expectancy predicted intention across both groups, while fear of dependency was negatively associated with intention. Privacy concerns strengthened the relationship between social influence and intention, and fear of dependency strengthened the relationship between performance expectancy and intention among experienced users. The moderating association of privacy concerns did not differ significantly by experience, whereas the moderating association of fear of dependency did.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Concerns about privacy and dependency were associated with the conditions under which older adults found SHTs compelling, suggesting that endorsement from trusted others and clear evidence of functional benefit may matter most for those who hold such concerns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Worried, deterred, and still interested: Psychological barriers and older adults’ intentions to adopt smart home technologies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home- and community-based services (HCBS) are central to Taiwan’s long-term care (LTC) system, yet some users show limited service use after entering the system. This study examined predictors of two patterns of limited HCBS use: low utilization and early dropout.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study analyzed administrative LTC records from Pingtung County, Taiwan, among cases entering the LTC system during 2019–2021: 17,517 in the low-utilization analysis and 18,678 in the early-dropout analysis. Low utilization was defined as service use in the lowest quartile of service-use days per 30 follow-up days, and early dropout as case closure within 90 days. Bootstrap-enhanced least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (BoLASSO) was applied, followed by multivariable logistic regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Low utilization was associated with care arrangements and entry pathways, including institutional residence, use of a paid migrant caregiver, co-residence with a nonfamily caregiver, and entry via the 1966 hotline. Early dropout occurred in 11.4% of cases and was associated with cancer, oxygen-related care needs, severe pain, underweight, unintentional weight loss, and inability to complete short-term memory assessment. Service-provider referral was associated with lower odds of both outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Low utilization and early dropout showed distinct predictor patterns: the former was more closely associated with care resources and entry pathways, whereas the latter was associated with health instability and recent decline. Distinguishing these patterns may inform more tailored care management and service delivery based on users’ needs and care contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Service use after long-term care entry: low utilization and early dropout in Taiwan

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Many interventions have been developed to improve outcomes for frail inpatients. No reviews have comprehensively mapped out these outcomes. This paper aims to assess the range and consistency of outcomes reported in interventional studies involving frail adult inpatients and identify whether the outcomes were patient-reported.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review of interventional studies involving frail adult inpatients from 2000 to 2026 was conducted, using the following databases: MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). All reported outcomes were extracted and catalogued to assess reporting range and consistency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From 74 included studies, 545 outcomes were identified and categorised into 43 domains. Among 545 outcomes, physical performance was the most frequently reported domain (n = 69, 12.7%), followed by mortality/survival (n = 43, 7.9%) and quality of life (QoL) (n = 36, 6.6%). Of the 74 included studies, mortality/survival was reported in 33 studies (44.6%), followed by physical performance (n = 27; 36.5%), and QoL (n = 26; 35.1%). Nearly half of the domains (44.2%) were measured in only one to three studies, including those directly related to the hospital experience. Of the 545 outcomes, 141 (25.9%) were classified as patient-reported outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There was heterogeneity and inconsistency in outcomes reported across interventional studies involving frail inpatients. This limits comparability and synthesis of study findings. The development of a core outcome set informed by the priorities of patients and caregivers, alongside healthcare professionals, would enhance the consistency, relevance, and quality of frailty research and better support patient-centred care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Range and Consistency of Reported Outcomes in Interventional Studies involving Frail Inpatients: A Systematic Review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Research on dementia care remains largely urban-centric, with limited understanding about the lived experiences and needs of people with cognitive impairment and dementia in rural communities. This scoping review aimed to understand the care priorities, service needs, and lived experiences of rural older adults with cognitive impairment and dementia in Canada.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following Arksey and O’Malley’s scoping review framework, we searched CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science for journal articles published from January 2015 to January 2025. Two reviewers independently screened the articles and extracted data from the relevant articles. We used reflexive thematic analysis to analyze the data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The scoping review identified 616 initial articles, with 16 relevant studies included in our review. Four interconnected themes were identified: i) complex navigational pathways and barriers in rural dementia care; ii) limited dementia knowledge creates challenges across the disease trajectory; iii) gaps in access to dementia-related services and supports; and iv) dementia-related stigma, fear, and social isolation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings revealed critical challenges in navigating rural dementia care, where geographical distance, misinformation, limited services, and dementia-related stigma exacerbate cognitive care disparities. Addressing these challenges requires ingenuity and prioritizing lived experience research to inform community-relevant solutions. Strategic investment and implementation science are needed to co-design, implement, and evaluate navigational support models and interdisciplinary dementia care hubs to improve rural access. Advancing rural dementia care requires moving beyond documenting challenges to evaluating scalable population-level interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Understanding the Care Priorities, Service Needs, and Lived Experiences of Rural Older Adults with Dementia and Cognitive Impairment in Canada: A Scoping Review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Workplace violence (WPV) in healthcare has increased over the last decade, yet limited evidence exists to guide home health agency (HHA) prevention efforts. This study examined HHA leaders and staff WPV experiences, including the type of violence, risk factors, and prevention strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted one-on-one semi-structured phone interviews with a purposive HHA sample of (a) 105 leaders, each representing a different organization, between November 2020-December 2022 and (b) 28 staff from five agencies between April 2023-August 2025. The socioecological framework guided the thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Leaders and staff contrasted the solitary, uncontrolled, and unpredictable HHA work environment with institutional healthcare contexts. HHA staff experiences reflected three types of WPV (i.e., criminal intent, violence perpetrated by the patient or others in the home, ideological violence perpetrated by the public). WPV risk factors spanned all domains of the socioecological framework. HHA staff and leaders described individual- and organizational-level WPV prevention strategies that targeted risk factors across framework domains. There was an absence of prevention strategies initiated at the community- and societal-level (e.g., WPV prevention legislation). Organizational strategies extended beyond annual staff training to include patient-specific safety plans, employing safety escorts, and discharge protocols for patient non-compliance with safety plans.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fostering HHA staff safety within the context of service delivery is complex and multi-dimensional. Findings emphasized the importance of a comprehensive approach that is tailored to the HHA’s community and populations served and a need for societal-level policies addressing WPV prevention and mitigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Workplace Violence in Home Health: Staff and Leadership Experiences and Strategies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical exercise is widely recognized as an effective non-pharmacological intervention that improves not only functional capacity, but also cognition and quality of life in older adults. However, the molecular pathways through which it influences aging-related processes remain incompletely understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize current evidence on the effects of structured physical exercise intervention on molecular biomarkers associated with inflammation and oxidative stress in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Randomized controlled trials which included participants ≥65 years old were identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 50 reports (4,379 participants) were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 38 of them in the different meta-analyses performed. Exercise interventions ranged from 8 weeks to 12 months and included aerobic, resistance, and multicomponent training. Pooled analyses indicated modest but significant reductions in C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and high-sensitivity CRP, as well as increases in IL-10. Effects on other pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and TNF-α, were inconsistent across studies. Evidence from a limited number of trials (n = 6) also suggested improvements in redox balance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, structured physical exercise demonstrates a moderate immunomodulatory and antioxidant effect in older adults, although bias was moderate to high. PROSPERO registry: CRD420251006248.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Impact of supervised physical exercise on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Compared to other age groups, older adults are often marginalized in the design processes of digital technologies leading to digital and social exclusion. While these aspects have been discussed in several reviews, an overarching perspective on how older adults are involved in Participatory Approaches (PA) in technology and innovation development is currently missing. This scoping review of reviews provides an overarching view on the narratives, trends, and gaps in PA in different fields of innovation, and proposes future research and practice directions. The study followed the Arksey & O’Malley’s protocol for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR checklist as the reporting guideline. Seven databases were screened for studies with a thematic focus on older adults, applying PA in technology and technology-related innovation, and published between 2014-2024. Twenty-two reviews were included. PA with older adults have seemingly evolved over the years with an increased focus on values equity, empowerment, power-sharing, and mutual learning. Nevertheless, deficit narratives on aging and ageism still constrain meaningful participation. A "participation gap" persists in which: terminology remains inconsistent; older adults are predominantly assigned roles of informants or testers rather than co-designers or equal partners; methods are mainly data-extractive; marginalized subgroups remain systematically underrepresented; and the technology scope remains predominantly care-centric. Identified gaps highlight the need for standardizing meaningful participation by creating a seal of quality for participatory approaches, improved reporting, and stronger inclusion of underrepresented populations and life domains of older persons.</jats:p>
title: Participatory Approaches with Older Adults in Technology and Innovation Research: A Scoping Review of Reviews

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An older subjective age is associated with worse cognitive health outcomes. Less is known about subjective age and cognitive function in daily life. The present study examines whether (1) baseline subjective age relates to momentary cognitive performance and nightly evaluations of subjective age and cognition, (2) daily cognitive performance relates to nightly evaluations of subjective age, and (3) nightly subjective age and cognition covary.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (N = 292, age range 40-70) reported on their subjective age at baseline, completed three cognitive tasks (Dot Memory, Symbol Search, Multiple Object Tracking) three times a day, and reported their nightly subjective age and perceived cognition for eight days.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multilevel growth models revealed that older baseline subjective age was associated with older nightly subjective age (b = 39.69, SE = 5.43, p &lt;.001), worse nightly subjective cognition (b = 24.175, SE = 5.598, p &lt;.001), and greater intraindividual variability in processing speed (b = 0.23, SE = 0.06, p &lt; .001). Additionally, nightly reports of older subjective age were associated with worse nightly subjective cognition (BP: -0.206, SE = 0.02, p &lt;.001; WP: b = -0.355, SE = 0.053, p&lt; .001). Baseline subjective age was unrelated to mean-level cognitive performance, and objective cognitive performance was unrelated to nightly subjective age.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Baseline subjective age did not relate to momentary cognitive performance, whereas both baseline levels and nightly fluctuations in subjective age were consistently linked to nightly perceptions of cognitive functioning, underscoring their relevance for understanding everyday cognitive experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Moment-to-Moment Performance and Nightly Subjective Assessments: Multi-Timescale Associations Between Subjective Age and Cognitive Function

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Racial and ethnic inequities in U.S. healthcare extend beyond insurance and access, yet less is known about how they vary across domains of healthcare experience and whether public insurance mitigates these inequities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Using four waves (2014–2020) of Health and Retirement Study data (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 16,088), this study examines disparities in satisfaction, affordability, accessibility, and preference concordance among middle-aged and older adults.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results show domain-specific disparities: Black, Hispanic, and “Other” respondents had higher odds of unmet healthcare preferences than non-Hispanic White respondents, while affordability gaps persisted. Differences in overall satisfaction were largely attenuated after adjustment, whereas Black respondents reported fewer accessibility barriers. Medicaid mitigated some disparities, particularly for Hispanic respondents in affordability and preference concordance, whereas Medicare showed limited moderating effects, with gains in satisfaction being more evident among non-Hispanic White respondents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, inequities persist beyond socioeconomic and health differences, highlighting structural and interpersonal factors in shaping healthcare experiences.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Life-space mobility reflects the extent and independence with which older adults move within their environments and is an integrative indicator of functional capacity and social participation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine associations of physical performance and daytime sleepiness with life-space mobility among community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional study was conducted among 403 older adults in Chile. Life-space mobility was assessed using the Life-Space Assessment (LSA), physical performance with the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), and daytime sleepiness with the Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Pearson correlations and multivariable linear regression were used to evaluate associations adjusting for age and sex.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Better physical performance and lower daytime sleepiness were associated with greater life-space mobility in bivariate analyses. In adjusted models, physical performance remained associated, whereas daytime sleepiness was not.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Physical performance is an important
                      <jats:bold>correlate</jats:bold>
                      of life-space mobility and may serve as an indicator of functional vulnerability in older adults.
                    </jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) play a critical role in coordinating health-related social services such as nutrition and medical transportation for older adults in their communities, yet their formal engagement with health care entities varies widely. This study examines organizational characteristics of AAAs associated with their shift to contracting with health care organizations. The study analyzed data using repeated waves of the National Survey of AAAs and the Community-Based Organization-Health Care Contracting Survey. Logistic regression assessed how organizational characteristics are associated with contract formation. Findings reveal that shifting into formal contracting was more likely for independent non-profit AAAs, those AAAs that provided care transition services, and AAAs with high annual budgets. Higher proportion of funding received from the Older Americans Act was negatively associated with a change in contracting status. This study suggests that organizational autonomy, financial stability, and diverse funding streams are associated with a higher capacity for entering into health care contracts.</jats:p>
title: The Shift to Social Care Contracting Between Health Care Entities and Community-Based Organizations

records.abstract: <jats:p>The use of digital tools in reminiscence interventions has increased in recent years, encompassing multimedia platforms, virtual reality (VR), digital life storybooks, and interactive applications. Yet, evidence regarding the effectiveness of digital reminiscence-based interventions remains limited. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesise the existing evidence on digital reminiscence-based interventions in care homes, with a focus on: (i) their development and evaluation; (ii) the extent to which they address cultural diversity and inclusivity; (iii) the support provided to end users; and (iv) the barriers and facilitators influencing their implementation. A systematic search of five databases (MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, PsycINFO, PubMed, Web of Science), and three grey literature sources (BASE, King’s Fund Database, PsyArXiv) was undertaken. Reference lists of key papers were also hand-searched. Studies of all methodologies (qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods) were included. Sixteen studies involving 365 participants met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were grouped into: (i) digital reminiscence, (ii) digital life story, and (iii) immersive VR. Reminiscence and life story interventions improved emotional wellbeing and social engagement, while VR mainly supported stimulation and mood. Stakeholder involvement in design of technology was limited, especially for people with dementia, and reporting on cultural diversity was minimal. Variation in intervention design and outcomes limited conclusions on overall effectiveness. Implementation facilitators were ability to personalise content, care provider/home manager support, staff engagement and training, and family involvement. Barriers included technology usability, organisational infrastructure and support, workforce knowledge and capacity, and difficulties integrating into routine care practices. Digital reminiscence generally improved wellbeing, mood, cognition, communication, social interaction, although findings were mixed and limited by small samples, and varied intervention designs and outcome measures. Future research should prioritise co-creation with people with dementia, families, and staff; include more diverse populations across the disease trajectory; and explore sustainable integration into routine care practice.</jats:p>
title: Digital Reminiscence-Based Interventions to Enhance Social Interaction of People With Dementia in Care Homes: A Scoping Review

<jats:p>
                    As the global population of people with dementia increases, the demand for best practice dementia care is growing. Textiles have the potential to assist with interacting with people with dementia and provide benefits in dementia care settings. However, there is currently limited understanding of, or experience with, the specific challenges, considerations and design of interactive textile products for people with moderate to advanced dementia. This exploratory qualitative study aimed to explore the perspectives of using interactive textiles with people with dementia. Seven sets of interactive textiles were tested for usability with nine people with dementia, followed by post-testing interviews. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with care partners and healthcare professionals to understand the effects of interactive textiles in two care settings. In total, 27 people were interviewed, including people with dementia (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 9), informal care partners (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 5), formal care partners/staff (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 2), and healthcare professionals (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 11), from a residential care home, a daycare centre, and a university located in southeastern Australia. The findings highlighted several benefits of interactive textiles, including assisting interactions, facilitating communication, providing sensory stimulation, supporting reminiscence, and promoting positive emotions such as reducing stress and anxiety. Participants suggest textiles can be used to provide engagement, describing the importance of forging connections between people with dementia and their past, bolstering familiar associations, emotional relations, and recognition of personal preferences. These insights informed design considerations and recommendations for creating interactive textiles that offer playful and meaningful activities for people with dementia.
                  </jats:p>
title: Understanding the Benefits of Textiles in Facilitating Interactions for People With Dementia: An Exploration of Design Considerations and Recommendations

records.abstract: <jats:p>Honoring individual preferences, like going outside, can enhance the health of nursing home (NH) residents living with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD). Although a hallmark of person-centered care, honoring ADRD residents’ preferences is often restricted when they are perceived to be high-risk for harm by NH staff. Accessible and efficient strategies are needed to help NH staff balance harmful risks to health and safety against the residents’ right to make autonomous choices, especially in under-resourced rural areas. This pilot study (NCT05618678) evaluated the feasibility of Decision-making In aGing and demeNtIa for auTonomY (DIGNITY), a multi-faceted and innovative, theory-based, person-centered risk management intervention aimed at assisting NH staff in respecting the preferences of rural residents living with ADRD, while optimizing safety. Feasibility was assessed using retention rates, staff surveys, and qualitative feedback. Fifty-two NH staff participated (88.7% female, 83.3% White, 94.3% non-Hispanic, and 48% with ≥6 years NH experience), with a 79% retention rate and 87.8% survey response rate. In the DIGNITY group, average scores (on Likert scale of 1–5) indicated high feasibility (3.99), acceptability (4.19), and appropriateness (4.24). Qualitative feedback highlighted the value of in-person training and telemonitoring sessions. The high ratings for feasibility, acceptability, and appropriateness of DIGNITY show its potential for supporting NH staff to more confidently provide person-centered care for ADRD residents.</jats:p>
title: Feasibility of the DIGNITY Intervention to Support Person-Centered Risk Management  in Rural Nursing Homes

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Greater age deviation (AgeDev), in which a person’s biological age is older than their chronological age, is associated with worse cognitive performance. Most findings, however, rely on lab-administered cognitive measures and do not account for time-ordered effects of practice. The present study leveraged a measurement burst dataset to examine six distinct features of cognitive performance (peak performance, change in peak performance, intraindividual variability, forgetting, retest-related gains), and explored whether individual differences in these features can be predicted by AgeDev. In a sample of 139 adults aged 25-65, baseline AgeDev (Horvath1, Horvath2, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge), DunedinPACE, and SystemsAge were derived from DNA methylation. Across four annual high-frequency assessment bursts, processing speed and working memory were assessed via a Symbol Search and N-Back task, respectively. Using Bayesian Double Exponential Models (BDEMs), we found that baseline peak performance was lower for individuals with greater AgeDev, DunedinPACE, and chronological age. Interestingly, individuals with greater AgeDev and faster DunedinPACE showed greater retest-related gains within and across bursts. Neither AgeDev nor chronological age predicted differences in cognitive change across time. Individuals with greater AgeDev showed more intraindividual variability in processing speed. Finally, greater chronological age (but not AgeDev) was linked with more forgetting between bursts in both tasks. These findings underscore the value of multidimensional indices of cognitive performance. Importantly, even in a sample spanning young adulthood through early old age, such indices may provide unique information regarding the nature of longitudinal patterns in cognition associated with chronological or biological aging.</jats:p>
title: Exploring Epigenetic Aging and Cognitive Change in Middle Adulthood

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Frailty and cognitive decline are common among older adults, increasing risks of disability and loss of independence. We have previously demonstrated in mice that short session (≤10 minute) high-intensity interval training (HIIT) is an effective intervention for frailty, but benefits for cognitive function and reducing hallmarks of aging have not been examined. Thus, we studied 24-month-old female C57BL/6J mice from our previous study that remained sedentary or performed a 10-minute HIIT regimen 3-days-a-week for 8 weeks. We found HIIT improved cognitive aspects including an increase in T-maze alternation % and novel object recognition, but no differences were observed in Barnes maze or light-dark preference. To explore HIIT impacts on the hallmarks of aging, we examined liver, gastrocnemius muscle, and cortex brain tissues for mitochondria expression, autophagy, cellular senescence, and telomere length. HIIT increased expression of mitochondrial complexes I and V, as well as PGC1α and SIRT3 in all tissues. Autophagy marker beclin was elevated across all tissues, while p62 was increased in liver and muscle but not in the cortex, and LC3-II was lower in muscle and liver. Senescence marker p16 was lower in HIIT muscle and liver, whereas p21 decreased in liver but increased in muscle. Telomere lengths were greater in liver, but no changes in muscle or cortex. Additionally, within the group of sedentary mice, we identified differences in hallmarks of aging that potentially underlie frailty as measured using different mouse frailty assessment tools. These results highlight the potential for multi-tissue geroprotective benefits of short session HIIT to reduce frailty and improve cognition for healthy aging.</jats:p>
title: Hallmarks of Aging Associate with High Intensity Interval Training Benefits and Frailty in Female C57Bl/6J Mice

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Although mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) is involved in aging and age-related neurodegenerative diseases, the impact of ALDH2 on age-related cognitive deficits and its underlying mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to explore the effects of ALDH2 on cognitive deficits in D-galactose-induced aging mice and illustrate the potential molecular mechanisms. We treated D-galactose-induced aging mice with Alda-1 (a potent agonist of ALDH2) for eight weeks and observed the alterations in behavior, levels of oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, mitochondrial function, and expression of mitochondrial biogenesis-related genes. The results revealed that Alda-1 alleviated neuropathological changes in the hippocampus and ameliorated cognitive deficits in D-galactose-induced aging mice. Administration of Alda-1 further reduced the levels of 4-HNE, MDA, 3-NT, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β; enhanced Mn-SOD and CAT activities; increased GSH and ATP levels and mitochondrial content; and upregulated PGC-1α/NRF-1/TFAM expression in the hippocampus of D-galactose-induced aging mice. Moreover, in D-galactose-treated HT22 cells, we found that the SIRT1 inhibitor EX527 reversed the Alda-1-induced upregulation of PGC-1α, suggesting that the Alda-1-induced upregulation of PGC-1α is associated with SIRT1 signaling. Collectively, Alda-1 ameliorated cognitive deficits in D-galactose-induced aging mice by reducing neuroinflammation, enhancing antioxidative capability, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis, and modulating the SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling pathway.</jats:p>
title: Alda-1 Alleviates the Cognitive Deficits in D-galactose-induced Aging Mice by Regulating Oxidative Stress, Neuroinflammation, and Mitochondrial Biogenesis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Against the backdrop of the “Dual Carbon” goals and accelerated population aging, changes in household demographic structure may influence household carbon emissions; however, existing research has not fully examined these effects and their heterogeneity at the micro household level. This study aims to investigate the impact of population aging on household carbon emissions and its heterogeneity based on Chinese household microdata.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the 2018 China General Social Survey (CGSS), this study employed the STIRPAT model and OLS regression. It characterizes population aging from three dimensions—“whether there are elderly members”, “proportion of elderly members”, and “average age of elderly members”—to examine its impact on total household carbon emissions, direct carbon emissions, and indirect carbon emissions, and further analyzes the heterogeneity of urban-rural, regional, climate conditions, as well as the mediating effect of household expenditure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study found a significant negative correlation between population aging and household carbon emissions, with the “structural effect” being stronger than the “age effect”. Households with elderly members have significantly reduced carbon emissions, and the higher the proportion of elderly members, the more significant the reduction in household carbon emissions. The impact of population aging on indirect carbon emissions is stronger than that on direct carbon emissions, indicating that it mainly exerts its effect by reducing expenditure and adjusting consumption structure. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the reduction in household carbon emissions caused by population aging is more pronounced in rural, central, and northern China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging has reduced household carbon emissions, which is of significant value for low-carbon governance. Policymakers should incorporate population aging into the household emission reduction framework and consider urban-rural and regional differences to promote differentiated low-carbon policy design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The impact of population aging on household carbon emissions and its heterogeneity: evidence from CGSS 2018 data in China

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Elderly people may need to stay in nursing home for various reasons. Separation from family may affect depression and perceived social support in older adults. This study aimed to investigate the effect of video communication on depression and perceived social support in nursing home residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This quasi-experimental study was conducted in 2022 on 61 older adults in nursing homes in Tabriz, Iran, using cluster sampling. Participants were randomly assigned to intervention (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 29) and control (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 32) groups. The intervention group received weekly video calls with family over two months alongside routine visits; while the Control group received routine visits only. Depression and perceived social support were assessed at baseline and after two months using Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) and Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      After the intervention, the mean depression score in intervention group was significantly lower than control group (Effect size = 0.87,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.001). The mean perceived social support score (Effect size = 0.67) in the intervention group was significantly higher compared to the control (Effect size = 0.67,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.01).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Video calls with family were associated with reduced depressive symptoms and increased perceived social support among nursing home residents. These findings show that video communication can be used in nursing homes to enhance the short-term well-being of residents.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mobility is fundamental to healthy ageing and quality of life, as it enables older adults to continue participating in all spheres of life, including social, cultural, civic, spiritual, and economic activities. This study explored and compared the perspectives of Canadian and Nigerian older adults regarding life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline. The two distinct national contexts provided insight into mobility decline between high-income and low-resource settings shaped by unique cultural, economic, and policy environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We recruited eighteen Canadian and eighteen Nigerian community-dwelling older adults from diverse sociodemographic strata through community-based organisations. Using a qualitative description design, we interviewed the participants about their experiences with and observations about mobility decline. The transcripts were coded and analysed using conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 36 participants aged 65 to 89 years, 47.2% were women, 66.7% had a spouse or partner, and 86.1% were middle-income earners. We categorised findings into four domains: demographic, socioeconomic, sociocultural, and socioenvironmental factors. Demographic factors such as older age, ageism, women’s gender roles, and singlehood or widowhood were perceived to influence mobility decline among older adults negatively. However, most Canadian participants perceived no gender-related influence, highlighting the cultural differences in perspectives between the two groups. Socioeconomic factors (education, occupation type, and income), sociocultural factors (traditional dietary patterns, religious practices, and social participation), and socioenvironmental factors (urban versus rural living conditions, housing, and climatic challenges) were also perceived to influence the mobility trajectories of older adults. Most Canadians perceived poorer mobility among rural dwellers, while Nigerians believed the converse. We also documented the recommendations that participants made for mitigating mobility decline, including their advocacy for supportive environments and policies that recognise the unique sociodemographic contexts of older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sociodemographic factors may disproportionately influence mobility decline. Policymakers can enhance equity in ageing experiences by implementing age-friendly community initiatives that support the mobility of older adults, especially in low-resource and rural areas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline: a comparative qualitative study of older adults’ perspectives in Canada and Nigeria

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An increase in foreign-born workers in nursing homes (NHs) has challenged first-line managers to implement language initiatives for their staff. Evidence regarding foreign-born care workers’ experiences of language support initiatives is still scarce. Thus, the aim of the study was to explore and describe the experiences of a language development intervention “Talk about Work” from the perspective of first-line managers (FLMs), language advocates and participating care staff.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An explorative qualitative study using on-going evaluation methods following the intervention “Talk about Work.” The intervention consisted of eight workshops intended to strengthen language and professional competence within health and social care. Semi-structured focus-group interviews were conducted with FLMs (3), language advocates (5), and caring staff including language assistants (20) at NHs. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify three main categories and seven subcategories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The educational material was suitable for caring staff, and FLMs found it beneficial also for future education plans. They could repeat topics, introduce new ones, and continue the intervention at different paces. Addressing Swedish language skills at work was perceived as sensitive, and the initiative made it easier to speak about language competences. Challenges for FLMs included finding staff with the right competences to lead the initiative. Language advocates asked for closer collaboration with FLMs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The intervention “Talk about Work” was considered appropriate for and was well received by all participating groups in the study. Moreover, FLMs could use the material for continued language initiatives at NHs. To improve language and communication skills among caring staff in multi-cultural contexts, there is a need to find staff with the right competences to lead language development initiatives as well as to provide resources to implement them.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Experiences from a language development intervention in nursing homes from the perspective of first-line managers, language advocates and care staff: a qualitative study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly prescribed, particularly in outpatient settings by general practitioners. In older patients with polypharmacy, inappropriate DOAC prescribing represents a major patient safety concern, potentially leading to therapeutic failure or preventable harm. To assess the quality and safety of DOAC prescriptions at hospital admission and discharge among older adults in 2023. Secondary objectives were to identify factors associated with inappropriate prescribing, characterize underlying prescribing errors, and compare these findings with data from 2018.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a prospective, observational, multicentre study across three French university hospitals, including departments of cardiology, internal medicine, post-emergency, and acute geriatrics. Older adults who were taking DOACs prior to admission and hospitalized for >24 hours were consecutively enrolled between November 2022 and May 2023. Appropriateness was defined according to European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines. Predictive factors were analyzed using logistic regression, and comparisons with 2018 data were made using χ² tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 536 eligible patients (mean age 84.1± 8.5 years; 50.6% women), 421 were included in the primary analysis. Most received apixaban (70.1%) for atrial fibrillation (83.6%). Inappropriate prescriptions were identified in 32.0% on admission and 24.9% at discharge (p = 0.004). Age >80 years (OR=1.80, CI95%= 1.20-2.72) and serum creatinine >133 µmol/L (OR=1.84, CI95%= 1.13-2.98) were associated with admission inappropriateness; age >80 years remained a discharge risk factor (OR=2.71, CI95%= 1.63-4.61), while weight <60 kg was protective (OR=0.42, CI95%= 0.25-0.69). No significant changes were observed compared to 2018.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Inappropriate DOAC prescribing during hospital transitions remains common in older adults, driven by advanced age and impaired renal function. The absence of substantial improvement since 2018 suggests that further efforts to optimize DOAC prescribing are warranted. Future interventions, including pharmacist-led medication reviews and integrated prescribing tools, could be considered to improve DOAC prescribing appropriateness in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical trial not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Appropriateness prescriptions of direct oral anticoagulants in hospital in 2023 in the older population: a prospective observational multicenter study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mealtimes in long-term care facilities are complex and serve multiple purposes. They provide opportunities for participation and learning, involving residents, relatives and healthcare professionals, each with unique circumstances. Participation and learning are central to healthy ageing. Healthcare professionals play a key role in enabling participation and learning among those involved, although these opportunities may be shaped by their perceptions and attitudes. Therefore, this study aimed to explore healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning among residents, their relatives, and colleagues related to mealtime situations in long-term care facilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews with 23 healthcare professionals (nursing assistants, licensed practical nurses, and registered nurses) working in long-term care facilities in a municipality in south-eastern Sweden. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Three themes were generated: (1)
                      <jats:italic>Shaped by relationships and circumstances</jats:italic>
                      , (2)
                      <jats:italic>Rewarding yet challenging</jats:italic>
                      , and (3)
                      <jats:italic>Prerequisites influence opportunities.</jats:italic>
                      Participation and learning related to mealtime situations manifested in various ways and to differing degrees, from extensive to almost non-existent. It was a balancing act for the healthcare professionals managing multiple challenges to enable participating and learning; however, residents and relatives were seldom invited to engage in this problem-solving. For participation and learning to occur, prerequisites were required at all levels in the organisation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthcare professionals perceive that participation and learning among residents, relatives, and colleagues in long-term care facilities do occur, but to varying degrees and are associated with multiple challenges. Drawing on a learning model, such as Illeris, can help identify which components need to be developed, which together with a deeper understanding and implementation of person-centredness, could contribute to increased participation and learning, and thereby to the wellbeing of residents, relatives, and healthcare professionals. However, this approach must permeate the entire organisation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning related to mealtimes in long-term care facilities: an interview study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Incontinence is a chronic condition that affects millions of adults over the age of 65 in the United States. This study estimates the direct medical costs of incontinence for this population and identifies some possible root causes driving these costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective analysis relied on administrative claims data from the 2018 Medicare Limited Data Set. The cost analysis was limited to fee-for-service (FFS) Medicare beneficiaries over the age of 65 enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B. Our analysis of urinary tract infections (UTIs) relied on a Medicare Advantage dataset from 2016 to 2018 that included service and drug costs. We used diagnosis codes and place-of-service codes from the 2018 claims experience to identify incontinent members and their respective care setting. We used propensity score matching of incontinent and non-incontinent members to estimate the incremental cost of incontinence, controlling for age, gender, regional state groupings, and 79 comorbidities based on ICD-10CM codes, categorized into 9 disease groups. We also created an event study of UTIs to explore whether the cost of a UTI episode differs based on the presence of incontinence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On average, direct medical costs for incontinent members were $404 per member per month (PMPM) in 2018 USD higher than their non-incontinent counterparts in the same care setting. This gap rises to $968 PMPM when averaged over all members across all four care settings because it accounts for the disproportionate migration of incontinent members into more intensive and expensive care settings. A significant driver of these costs is the higher prevalence of urinary tract infections (UTIs) among incontinent members. Using an event study of UTIs, we also find that the treatment costs for UTIs are 52% higher, on average, for incontinent members.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The direct medical cost of incontinence for adults over 65 is comparable in magnitude to other major chronic conditions such as obesity, cancer, and diabetes, yet receives far less policy and management attention. Payers and institutions can make meaningful gains in reducing this cost by investing in incontinence management strategies that reduce UTIs, support caregivers, and prevent transitions to higher-intensity care settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The direct medical cost of urinary and fecal incontinence by care settings for adults over 65 in the United States

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults frequently present to emergency departments (EDs) after falls or suspected head injury, often with multimorbidity, cognitive impairment, and uncertain injury timing. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) may support imaging decisions after mild traumatic brain injury, but age- and disease-related elevations may reduce specificity in older patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a single-center exploratory observational pilot study with prospective serum collection and retrospective clinical and imaging data abstraction in Poland from October 2023 to April 2024. Consecutive eligible patients aged ≥ 65 years presenting during the primary investigator’s clinical shifts were enrolled. Participants were classified as head injury sampled ≤ 24 h (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 47), head injury sampled > 24 h (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 7), or selected non-trauma presentations without documented head injury (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 41). GFAP and UCH-L1 were measured on the Abbott ARCHITECT platform. We assessed positivity at manufacturer decision limits (GFAP ≥ 35 pg/mL; UCH-L1 ≥ 400 pg/mL). All patients in the ≤ 24-h subgroup underwent head CT; the composite endpoint included acute traumatic intracranial hemorrhage or cerebral contusion and/or acute fractures of the skull, facial skeleton, or upper cervical spine.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GFAP positivity occurred in 91.5% (43/47), 100.0% (7/7; descriptive only), and 78.0% (32/41) of the three groups, respectively. UCH-L1 positivity occurred in 55.3% (26/47), 42.9% (3/7), and 26.8% (11/41). Nine of 47 patients (19.1%) in the ≤ 24-h subgroup had at least one CT-positive acute traumatic finding. GFAP showed a preliminary discriminatory signal (AUC 0.868; 95% CI 0.728–1.000), whereas UCH-L1 showed no apparent discrimination (AUC 0.488; 95% CI 0.222–0.755). A combined model yielded an AUC of 0.874 (95% CI 0.747–1.000), only minimally higher than GFAP alone. At the manufacturer GFAP decision limit, sensitivity was 100.0% (9/9; 95% CI 66.4–100.0) and specificity was 10.5% (4/38; 95% CI 2.9–24.8).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among selected older ED patients, positivity at manufacturer decision limits was frequent beyond documented head injury. GFAP showed a preliminary signal for the composite acute traumatic CT endpoint, but estimates were imprecise and specificity was very low; UCH-L1 added little diagnostic information. These findings support cautious, age- and context-aware interpretation and require external validation. They do not establish new clinical thresholds or effects on geriatric care pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Serum GFAP and UCH-L1 in selected older emergency department patients: positivity beyond documented head injury

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity is highly prevalent among older adults and is associated with functional decline, disability, cognitive impairment, and increased healthcare burden. However, traditional disease-count approaches may fail to capture the heterogeneity of multimorbidity patterns. This study aimed to identify cardiometabolic multimorbidity phenotypes and examine their associations with functional and cognitive outcomes among older Chilean adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional analysis was conducted using data from 2,031 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 60 years from the Chilean National Health Survey 2016–2017. Six objectively measured cardiometabolic conditions were included: diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, elevated total cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, and obesity. K-means cluster analysis was applied to identify multimorbidity phenotypes, and the number of clusters was selected combining elbow, silhouette, and clinical interpretability criteria. Functional outcomes included self-rated health assessed using the EQ-5D visual analogue scale (EQ-VAS), mobility limitations, difficulty performing usual activities, and pain/discomfort. Cognitive performance was assessed using the abbreviated Mini-Mental State Examination. Adjusted linear regression models controlling for age and sex were performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Overall, 53.5% of participants presented multimorbidity (≥ 2 conditions). Four multimorbidity phenotypes were identified: Low-burden (30.9%), Obesity-predominant (25.1%), Hypertension-dominant (22.1%), and Metabolic + obesity (21.9%). Significant between-group differences were observed for self-rated health (ANOVA
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.022), cognitive performance (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.0003), mobility limitations (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.005), difficulty performing usual activities (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.0008), and pain/discomfort (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.003). The phenotype structure was robust to the exclusion of metabolic syndrome in a sensitivity analysis (Adjusted Rand Index = 0.719). In adjusted analyses with the Low-burden phenotype as reference, the Hypertension-dominant phenotype was independently associated with greater pain/discomfort (β = 0.14, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.21; FDR-adjusted
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.011) and the Metabolic + obesity phenotype with higher Mini-Mental scores (β = 0.56, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.95; FDR-adjusted
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.039); an association between the Hypertension-dominant phenotype and lower self-rated health (β = -4.25, 95% CI -8.00 to -0.50) did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Distinct cardiometabolic multimorbidity phenotypes were differentially associated with functional and cognitive outcomes among older Chilean adults. These findings support the importance of phenotype-based approaches to improve risk stratification and promote more personalized strategies in geriatric care and healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cardiometabolic multimorbidity phenotypes and their associations with functional and cognitive outcomes in older Chilean adults: findings from the Chilean national health survey

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physicians treating older patients are frequently unaware of their patients’ personal attitudes towards life-sustaining measures like ventilation, resuscitation, feeding tubes, or ICU admission. In routine clinical practice, there is often little time for reflection prior to deciding in favor or against life sustaining measures in critical medical conditions.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>Although decisions for or against these measures should ideally be made jointly by the patient and the treating physician, factors like age, disease burden, social inclusion, and affective state may play an important role in the patient’s motivation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from 161 inpatients (mean age 82.0 years) on a geriatric ward were collected and analyzed. Patients were interviewed about their attitudes towards life-sustaining measures like ventilation, resuscitation, tube feeding, ICU admission, and dialysis. Four composite indices were formed by combining sign-aligned component variables: medical burden (age and Charlson Comorbidity Index), functional and cognitive impairment (Barthel Index, iADL, and MoCA), affective distress (Geriatric Depression Scale and Hamilton Depression Scale suicidality item), and social support (living situation, having children, and having friends). These indices with other covariates were then analyzed using a Bayesian Rasch item response model with latent regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, 14.3% refused all invasive life sustaining measures, whereas 33.8% wished to receive all of the measures listed above. Artificial nutrition was the most refused measure (refused by 53.4%), whereas ICU admission was the most commonly accepted measure (74.4%). Social support had no meaningful association with the decision to accept or refuse life-sustaining measures. Relevant predictors were primarily lower levels of affective distress, and secondarily better functional and cognitive performance and lower medical burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Even among older patients, only a minority completely reject life-sustaining measures, even though their life expectancy is often significantly reduced. Patient’s attitude towards life-sustaining measures appears to be related more strongly to affective state, functional performance, and medical burden than living situation or social inclusion. As the patient’s emotional and functional state can certainly be influenced by medical treatment, practitioners should bear this in mind and, where appropriate, reassess their patients’ attitude towards LSM once the aforementioned conditions have improved.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Registered with the clinical trial registry Deutsches Register Klinischer Studien.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Older patients and intensive care: factors that influence patients decisions on life sustaining measures
