<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background/objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging presents challenges for society and healthcare, notably in preventing sarcopenia, a condition that impairs older adults’ quality of life and functionality. This article reviews the current literature on dietary and exercise interventions to evaluate their effectiveness in managing sarcopenia and explore their integration in primary care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review was conducted under PRISMA guidelines by searching PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Embase, and the Cochrane Library via MeSH terms and the PICOS criteria. The analysis focused on randomized studies involving adults over 65 years of age that assessed nutritional and exercise interventions delivered in primary care settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Six studies, encompassing 444 participants in experimental groups and 226 in control groups, met the inclusion criteria. Combined interventions, physical exercise paired with nutritional supplementation, demonstrated notable improvements in muscle strength, physical function, and body composition. However, the results varied depending on the study design and adherence rates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multidimensional approaches within primary care show promising potential for slowing sarcopenia progression and enhancing quality of life among older adults. Despite encouraging findings, limited research in this area signals the need for further studies emphasizing personalized, sustainable strategies to optimize clinical implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Approach to sarcopenia in older adults: a systematic review of dietary and exercise interventions in the primary care setting

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity is prevalent among older adults, but its specific patterns and differential associations with impairments across intrinsic capacity (IC) domains remain under-explored. This study aimed to identify stable multimorbidity patterns in rural older adults using multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) combined with k-means clustering and to examine their independent associations with domain-specific IC impairments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 3,641 community-dwelling older adults with multimorbidity (≥ 2 of 15 chronic conditions) from rural China. MCA was used to reduce dimensionality, followed by k-means clustering to identify multimorbidity patterns. Multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, education, income, and smoking status, was used to estimate the associations between the identified patterns and impairments in each of the six IC domains (cognition, physical function, vitality, psychology, hearing, and vision), with the high metabolic burden pattern used as the reference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five stable multimorbidity patterns were identified: high metabolic burden (36.4%), musculoskeletal degenerative (28.4%), gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern (13.8%), cardiovascular-heart failure pattern (13.0%) and respiratory pattern (8.4%). Compared with the high metabolic burden pattern, the gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern was associated with higher odds of vitality impairment (OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.30–2.21); the cardiovascular-heart failure pattern was associated with higher odds of physical function impairment (OR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.11–1.77); and the gastrointestinal-tumor risk pattern, cardiovascular-heart failure pattern, and respiratory pattern were all associated with higher odds of psychological impairment (ORs from 1.61 to 2.27). The respiratory and gastrointestinal-tumor risk patterns were also associated with higher odds of hearing and visual impairments. Notably, the high metabolic burden pattern demonstrated the strongest risk for cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Distinct multimorbidity patterns are differentially associated with specific IC domain impairments. These findings support pattern-oriented risk stratification and targeted functional management in older adults, offering a practical framework for precision geriatric care in resource-limited rural settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Multimorbidity patterns and domain-specific intrinsic capacity impairments among rural older adults: a multiple correspondence analysis and k-means clustering study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community exergaming may help older adults remain physically active by combining movement, enjoyment, and social interaction, but less is known about whether observed changes persist after supervised delivery ends in real-world community settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated immediate and maintenance-related outcomes of the International Singapore Intergenerational National Games, a community-delivered exergaming program for older adults in Singapore. We examined positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, habit strength, physical activity, and exploratory implementation determinants aligned with the capability, opportunity, and motivation–behavior (COM-B) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a multi-wave observational evaluation from October 2025 to January 2026 among 280 older adults recruited from 14 senior activity centers or active aging centers in Singapore. Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately after an 8-week supervised training phase (T1), after a 4-week unsupervised free-play phase (T2), and at a later follow-up for selected measures in 6 centers (T3). Immediate within-person changes were examined using 2-tailed paired
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      tests. Maintenance-related trajectories were examined using adjusted linear mixed-effects models. Exploratory analyses examined whether COM-B–aligned capability, opportunity, and motivation composites were associated with physical activity trajectories.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants had a mean age of 72.54 (SD 6.15) years, and 77.1% (216/280) were female. From T0 to T1, mean positive mental health increased from 55.19 (SD 9.79) to 57.59 (SD 8.70; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.28;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), mean intrinsic motivation increased from 5.94 (SD 1.00) to 6.29 (SD 0.81; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.40;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), and mean habit strength increased from 3.34 (SD 1.11) to 3.81 (SD 0.84; Cohen
                      <jats:italic>dz</jats:italic>
                      =0.42;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). In adjusted mixed models, habit strength remained higher at T2 than at baseline (β=0.362, 95% CI .113-.611;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.005), and intrinsic motivation remained higher at T2 (β=0.397, 95% CI .156-.638;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.001) and T3 (β=0.305, 95% CI .009-.601;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04). Positive mental health was higher immediately after supervised training (β=4.140, 95% CI 2.169-6.111;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) and at T2 (β=7.390, 95% CI 5.370-9.410;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) than at baseline. Among the COM-B domains, only opportunity was associated with greater immediate posttraining physical activity improvement (time × opportunity interaction β=26.464, 95% CI 3.191-49.737;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), with no evidence of a sustained interaction at T2.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this observational evaluation, positive mental health, intrinsic motivation, and habit strength were higher at T2 than at baseline among respondents with available follow-up data, and intrinsic motivation was also higher at the selected-center T3 follow-up. Because this study lacked a control group and attrition increased over time, these findings represent observed longitudinal trajectories rather than causal evidence of program effectiveness. Opportunity-related supports such as access, reminders, routines, staff facilitation, and peer participation may be useful when community exergaming transitions from supervised delivery to reduced-intensity free play, although this interpretation remains exploratory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Community Exergaming and Maintenance-Related Outcomes in Older Adults: Multi-Wave Observational Evaluation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There is a thorough literature on the mental health consequences of discrimination exposure in adulthood, yet little work to date has situated such experiences within a relational, dyadic context. The present brief report analyzes two-wave longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS; 2018-2022) to determine whether individuals’ own or their intimate partner’s experiences of discrimination were associated with changes to anxiety symptoms, perceived stress, and/or self-esteem over a four-year period.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Methods and Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dyadic lagged dependent variable (LDV) models were estimated using a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework with full information maximum likelihood (FIML) methods to address missing data. A total of 1,484 individuals from 742 opposite-gender couples participated at both the 2018 and 2022 waves of data collection and comprised the analytic sample for this study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Individuals’ own exposure to everyday discrimination was associated with increased symptoms of anxiety and perceived stress, as well as with reduced self-esteem, over the four-year period. A dyadic partner’s exposure to everyday discrimination was associated with increased anxiety symptoms for men only, though post-hoc Wald tests failed to find a significant gender difference in effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Discrimination is a chronic psychosocial stressor with harmful consequences for mental health of affected individuals even in mid and later life. Moreover, limited evidence suggests that discrimination may have dyadic consequences as well, though these patterns are mixed. Future research is needed to determine interpersonal mechanisms for the findings of interest.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Dyadic discrimination and mental well-being among older Americans

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias represent a global public health concern, with persistent gaps in supports for individuals living with dementia and their unpaid care partners. This study synthesized promising community-based innovations that address these gaps and contribute to positive outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A rapid literature review was conducted to develop a framework for guiding the design and evaluation of community innovations for individuals living with dementia and their care partners. Four databases were searched using keywords related to dementia, care partners, community-based care, and quality outcomes. Twenty-two articles were included, each evaluating a community-based intervention for individuals with dementia and their care partners and reported outcomes. Cross-study thematic analysis identified programmatic factors associated with success.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The resulting framework comprises six programmatic factors of success, six design and implementation considerations, and four cross-cutting principles. Success factors included early intervention, triadic involvement in planning, individualized and person-centered approaches, multi-component interventions, community-building activities, and direct care partner resources and tools. Design and implementation considerations included target population, delivery models, co-design strategies, resource allocation and system incentives, geographic context, and impacts and outcomes. Core principles emphasize anti-stigma, accessibility, equity and intersectionality, and sustainability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Co-design and sustained community engagement were identified as central strategies for reducing stigma and fostering inclusive, dementia-supportive environments. The framework can be used to support the development, investment, and scalability of effective community-based supports for individuals living with dementia and care partners across diverse settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Community-based solutions: A principles-to-practice framework to support individuals living with dementia and their care partners

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Depression is a modifiable predictor of dementia, but the effects of addressing depression to improve cognition, especially psychosocial interventions, are understudied. The underlying relationships between depressive symptoms (DS) and cognitive function (CF) are also unclear. Most prior research has been observational, lacking insight into their interactions during interventions. This study examined the longitudinal relationships between DS and CF across psychosocial interventions in older adults, modeling changes as latent variables for more accurate estimations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study drew on participant data from JC JoyAge, a community stepped-care program for late-life mental health. Participants (≥60 years) with mild to moderate DS (N = 4,412) completed DS and CF assessments (e.g., attention, language, orientation, memory domains) before and after the program. Latent change score models were computed to examine changes in DS and CF as well as their interaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On average, participants’ DS and CF improved following intervention. A greater reduction in DS was associated with greater improvement in CF. Higher baseline CF predicted a greater reduction in DS, while a lower baseline DS predicted a greater improvement in global CF, attention, and memory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings demonstrated the bidirectional relationships between DS and CF and showed their shared improvements during psychosocial intervention. Treating depression is expected to benefit cognition, potentially preventing cognitive decline and dementia. Combining depression and cognition components in integrated intervention approaches may enhance their reciprocal response. Early intervention at a lower depression level may achieve greater cognitive benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The bidirectional relationship between depression and cognitive function in older adults: Evidence from a psychosocial intervention on late-life depression

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retirement transition (RT) is a dynamic process with individual heterogeneity. While the Resource-Based Dynamic Perspective (RBDP) highlights fluctuations in key resources, studies remain largely quantitative and cross-sectional. This study aims to identify distinct RT patterns and examine shifts in resource-related discourse over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative longitudinal design with computational augmentation tracked 12 Taiwanese near-retirees across five waves spanning six months pre- to six months post-retirement. Sixty qualitative transcripts were analyzed using longitudinal case methods, complemented by computational text mining (Sentence-BERT) to trace trajectories across six resource domains, including Health Issues, Life Control, Financial Status, Social Support, Emotional Response, and Lifestyle.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Within this sample, three analytically derived RT patterns were observed: a transition-centered pattern in Strategic Goal-Driven (Type I, n = 4), a U-shaped pattern in Structure and Social Role Reshaping (Type II, n = 4), and a crisis-driven peak in External Shock Response (Type III, n = 4). Text-mining results broadly converged with qualitative findings, particularly in the Life Control domain. At the individual level, convergence was observed for financial status and lifestyle, whereas divergence emerged when similar quantitative frequencies corresponded to different qualitative meanings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings extend RBDP by introducing resource diversion, in which family or contextual demands redirect personal resources, and a resource hierarchy highlighting the foundational role of physical health. Findings underscore the need for pathway-specific retirement support that accounts for culturally embedded caregiving obligations beyond conventional financial-planning approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mapping heterogeneity in retirement transition pathways: Integrating qualitative longitudinal and text mining analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Resident-to-resident aggression (RRA) is the most common form of elder mistreatment in long-term care settings. Although race/ethnicity is likely a contributing factor, research has been limited in examining the role of residents’ race and ethnicity in RRA. We sought to define and qualitatively examine the predisposing factors and acute precipitants of race/ethnicity-related resident-to-resident aggression (RE-RRA).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by the socioecological model, events-based perspective, and conceptual work on stigma-based aggression, we developed qualitative interview and data analytical guides. We conducted nine focus groups and twelve in-depth interviews with 81 nursing home staff from multiple clinical and non-clinical roles across two long-term care facilities on the U.S. East Coast. We coded qualitative data using a deductive thematic qualitative approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-RRA appeared to be a recurring interpersonal dynamic, though its full scope is likely under-detected and under-recognized. We identified five major types of RE-RRA, including physical violence, microaggression, social exclusion, and avoidance. Ten predisposing factors and eight acute precipitants uniquely contributed to RE-RRA, highlighting the importance of considering distinct race- and ethnicity-related elements in prevention research. We summarized our findings in a conceptual framework for RE-RRA that may be useful for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>RE-RRA is a distinct phenomenon shaped by identifiable predisposing and precipitating factors, offering opportunities for future prevention and intervention development. These findings underscore the importance of integrating RE-RRA within staff education, existing clinical governance structures, including incident reporting, and quality improvement processes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Exploring the Role of Race and Ethnicity in Resident-to-Resident Aggression: A Qualitative Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Palliative care (PC) consultation outcomes in nursing homes (NHs) are often assessed using health systems' clinical and utilization metrics rather than outcomes from the perspective of the key partners who provide and sustain it. This study was designed to identify meaningful PC consultation outcomes from the perspectives of NH staff, PC consultants, and NH/PC agency directors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a qualitative descriptive approach, the team conducted semi-structured interviews with key partners from 14 NHs in the Eastern United States. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using conventional content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (N = 33) included NH staff (e.g., primary care providers and nurses), PC consultants (e.g., PC physicians and PC nurse practitioners), and leaders (e.g., NH directors and PC agency directors). Key partners reported meaningful outcomes in four domains: resident, family, NH staff, and NH facility. Resident outcomes included goal-concordant care, symptom management, hospitalization rates, and understanding of care choices and control. Family outcomes included shared decision-making, understanding of the resident’s disease trajectory and management measures, and feeling supported. NH staff outcomes included capacity to provide high-quality care and emotional support. Lastly, NH facility outcomes included filling care gaps, facility reputation, and organizational morale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight multi-domain and interdependent PC consultation outcomes across residents, families, staff, and NH facilities that may be overlooked in existing evaluation frameworks. Future interventions and quality measures should incorporate these outcomes and ensure that residents’ and families’ perspectives are represented.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Identifying Palliative Care Consultation Outcomes in Nursing Homes: Insights from Key Partners

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.</jats:p>
title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This manuscript analyzes the literary, social and cultural representations of dementia in Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019). I contend that the authors’ accounts of their mothers’ struggle with dementia, from its onset to its end, function as living archives of personal and national history. I employ life writing, aging studies, and, to a lesser extent, historiography to examine the literary, social cultural, and historical dimensions of such experiences. I address the narrative construction of the mothers’ identity in later life by highlighting the role of archives and family memories in the context of contemporary South Africa. Thus, I aim to illustrate the instrumental role of life narratives in the creation of safe spaces for intergenerational dialogue and reconciliation with a troubled past on a personal and national level. I also contend that humanities-based inquiry brings to the fore the essential aspects of later life, thereby challenging the pathologizing medical in the representation of dementia, which often disregards the reality of old people as vessels of knowledge. Eventually, I showcase that illness life narratives function as accessible repositories of public knowledge that render visible the realities of aging.</jats:p>
title: Living History, Fading Minds: Dementia as the Gateway to Historical Past in South Africa via Antjie Krog’s Blood’s Inner Rhyme (2025) and Julia Martin’s The Blackridge House (2019)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ageism in healthcare contributes to undertreatment, dismissive communication, and age-based exclusions from care, yet no psychometrically validated, patient-reported measure captures older adults’ perceptions of age-based bias during clinical encounters. We developed and validated the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) scale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Items adapted from four validated discrimination measures plus two new items were administered to community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older in three independent, predominantly non-Hispanic White samples (Ns = 223, 349, 361) recruited through Prolific within the United States. Study 1 examined latent structure with exploratory factor analysis; Study 2 tested and refined the structure with confirmatory factor analysis; Study 3 confirmed the refined model and evaluated reliability, measurement invariance across gender, and construct validity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 2 indicated that a 20-item model fit poorly and that removing three items produced a refined 17-item model. Study 3 confirmed this model (CFI = .926, RMSEA = .058, SRMR = .057), with excellent reliability for Interpersonal Ageism and the total scale, good reliability for Institutional Ageism, full scalar invariance across gender, and coherent discriminant and convergent validity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development and Validation of the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) Scale: A Three-Study Investigation of Perceived Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism in Clinical Care

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As the prevalence of multimorbidity among older adults is rising, challenges regarding their end-of-life healthcare choices are increasingly relevant. To address knowledge gaps regarding decision-making, we explored how older adults with multimorbidity, their relatives and involved healthcare professionals experienced end-of-life healthcare choices, how their experiences related to each other and how these choices occurred in interactions between them over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a multiperspective, longitudinal, interview and observation study with a phenomenological and ethnographic approach. We followed nine six-month patient trajectories with eleven relatives and 58 healthcare professionals and conducted 73 observations of patient-healthcare professional interactions and 63 interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The meaning of end-of-life healthcare choices of older people with multimorbidity was essentially understood as an ongoing, entangled, existential and relational process, shaped by, yet also transcending, healthcare contexts. This process was characterized by four tensions: (i) the experience of not having a choice, but making decisions nonetheless; (ii) the existential experience and the medical gaze; (iii) the importance of relatives and their limited role in healthcare; and (iv) navigating fragmented healthcare with interrelated conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthcare professionals’ limited insight into patients’ and relatives’ personal, existential perspectives and relational contexts calls for a better exploration of their lifeworld to ensure the best possible alignment of healthcare decisions with patients’ and relatives’ needs and values. Older adults with multimorbidity are inadequately supported by fragmented healthcare systems, and efforts to improve this should consider existential, relational and systemic factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “I don’t know whether I really have choices”: a multiperspective and longitudinal exploration of healthcare choices of older adults with multimorbidity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hospital-to-home transitions constitute vulnerable periods during which health systems increasingly rely on unpaid care partners to help care recipients execute discharge plans. We examine how mutuality and incongruence within care partner-care recipient dyads may shape discharge preparedness and dyadic self-efficacy during care transitions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a secondary qualitative analysis of PROJECT ACHIEVE focus groups and key informant interviews with 248 participants (138 care recipients, 110 care partners) across six U.S. health systems, examining their experiences of hospital-to-home transitions. A multidisciplinary team conducted thematic analysis and compared themes across stakeholder groups, guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Interdependence Theory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Care recipients and care partners shared goals but often differed in their appraisals of discharge readiness and post-discharge roles. Three domains of incongruence emerged: (1) preparedness for transitions home, as care recipients prioritized going home despite ongoing symptoms while care partners worried about premature discharge and inadequate training; (2) burdensomeness and struggle for independence, as care recipients desired to preserve autonomy while care partners absorbed the emotional and practical strain of supporting such desires; and (3) role changes and evolving relational identities, as spouses and adult children assumed caregiving roles that disrupted prior identities in the relationship. Lower mutuality was linked to reduced dyadic self-efficacy and, consequently, increased risk of readmission.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight dyadic incongruence as a target for intervention in care transitions. Care strategies that assess care recipient-care partner mutuality may enhance dyadic self-efficacy and improve post-discharge outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Themes of Incongruence in the Relationships between Care Partners and Care Recipients During Discharge from Hospital to Home

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Understanding the factors that enable or hinder successful implementation is essential for improving patient outcomes. Hospital in Home (HiH) programs provide hospital-level care in patients' homes to reduce hospitalization, enhance satisfaction, and improve resource use. Within the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), 14 sites have implemented HiH programs, yet limited research has examined implementation within a large integrated system. This study identifies factors that can support or hinder HiH implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted interviews with 48 key informants across 14 VHA HiH sites. Guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) 2.0, we applied directed content analysis using a priori constructs, then developed site-level matrices to summarize findings and compare patterns across sites.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified 18 CFIR constructs—nine that primarily facilitated implementation and nine mixed factors that acted as both facilitators and barriers. Key facilitators included two Individual-level factors (HiH lead capability and motivation, team motivation), one Innovation factor (relative advantage of HiH), and four Implementation Process factors (planning, teaming, reflecting and evaluating, adapting). Mixed factors were mostly within the inner setting, reflecting medical center context, along with two Individual-level mixed factors (leader and recipient motivation).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>HiH programs hold strong potential to transform care for older adults, but success depends on addressing barriers and leveraging facilitators, particularly within the inner setting. Understanding key implementation determinants can enhance adoption, improve outcomes, and strengthen healthcare delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Identifying Contextual Factors affecting Hospital In Home Program Implementation within the Veterans Health Administration

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Limited Medicare literacy contributes to suboptimal plan selection and disparities in coverage outcomes among older adults, particularly in historically underserved communities. This study examined Medicare enrollment literacy, information access, and decision-making experiences among first-time Black Medicare beneficiaries in Southeast Queens, New York, using a convergent mixed-methods design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Quantitative data were collected through a community-based survey of first-time Medicare beneficiaries (N = 93). Descriptive statistics assessed Medicare literacy across a 15-item scale and examined information sources, decision support, and plan selection patterns. Qualitative data were obtained through three focus groups and four individual interviews (N = 16) with community navigators and Medicare enrollment professionals and were analyzed using thematic analysis. Document analysis examined the clarity, readability, and cultural relevance of commonly used Medicare materials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>More than half of participants demonstrated low Medicare literacy, and fewer than half reported confidence in comparing plans, understanding coverage differences, and estimating out-of-pocket costs. Most participants received assistance with enrollment decisions. Qualitative findings identified five themes: complexity and information overload, reliance on informal support networks, digital navigation barriers, confusion about coverage and costs, and the importance of trust and culturally relevant communication. Document analysis indicated that many materials were complex and relied heavily on insurance terminology, with limited cultural tailoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Limited Medicare literacy reflects both individual knowledge gaps and systemic barriers. Enhancing culturally responsive outreach, simplifying materials, and expanding community-based decision support may improve equitable enrollment outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Medicare Enrollment Literacy Among First-Time Black Beneficiaries: Insights From a Mixed-Methods Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Epistemic injustice, introduced by philosopher Miranda Fricker in 2007, refers to harm affecting individuals as knowers because of social prejudices and stereotyping. This leads to the partial or complete exclusion of certain individuals from knowledge building. People living with dementia are particularly vulnerable because cognitive impairments may reinforce assumptions about reduced credibility, marginalising their voices in clinical, social and family contexts and limiting opportunities to exercise epistemic agency. This research examines how people living with dementia experience epistemic injustice in everyday life and how it shapes their participation as knowers in clinical, social, and family contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with a conversational approach was conducted. Participants (N = 15) with a dementia diagnosis were interviewed in their homes or nursing homes. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed thematically to identify recurring patterns and meanings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three interconnected domains were identified: epistemic marginalisation in clinical encounters, everyday negotiation of competence and agency, and epistemic invalidation and silencing in interpersonal relationships. Participants often perceived these experiences as appropriate or expected rather than unjust, reflecting internalised stigma. Many felt their perspectives were no longer recognised as valuable, leading to withdrawal from care and communication and fewer opportunities to contribute their knowledge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Epistemic injustice extends beyond healthcare, affecting everyday and family interactions by progressively limiting opportunities for people living with dementia to participate as credible knowers. Its normalisation fosters self-silencing, perpetuating disempowerment and social exclusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “The right to be heard: exploring epistemic injustice in dementia care. A qualitative study”

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Speaking up about quality and safety issues can protect older people and support learning in health and social care systems. In aged care, staff work in diverse roles to deliver care to residents with complex care needs. This meta-ethnography aimed to synthesise evidence on staff experiences of raising concerns about quality and safety in long-term residential aged care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We included qualitative studies examining staff experiences of speaking up, incident reporting, and whistleblowing. Five databases were searched. The seven phases of meta-ethnography were used to translate first and second order constructs into third order constructs and a line-of-argument synthesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirteen articles of 11 studies were synthesised to reveal four third order constructs: 1. Sensemaking a concern, 2. Organisational cultures determine how they are voiced, heard and respond to, 3. Systemic resources shape and constrain possibilities for voicing, and 4. Normalisation of poor care and loss of moral agency in organisations that respond with indifference. Raising concerns was a dynamic, recursive process encompassing phases of recognising, voicing, and organisational responding. Where quality and safety issues were normalised, individualised, or met with limited action, staff described moral distress, disengagement, and, in some cases, exit from the organisation or sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Raising concerns in residential aged care is a dynamic process shaped by interrelated individual, organisational and systemic factors. Speaking up interventions need to go beyond skills training to address phases of recognising care quality issues and how organisations respond when they are raised.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A meta-ethnography of staff experiences of raising concerns about quality and safety in residential aged care

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A sense of Home is an important part of wellbeing for all peoples, and there are unique dimensions to Home for Indigenous elders. Yet, there is a dearth of literature exploring the experiences and perspectives of Indigenous peoples in aged residential care (ARC) settings, and even less so from the perspectives of Indigenous elders themselves. The objective of this scoping review is to investigate and synthesise literature on Indigenous conceptualisations of Home and Home features in ARC settings from Indigenous elders’ perspectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research design and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review was conducted through a systematic search of qualitative research from PubMed, PsycInfo, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar databases. A framework considering Home holistically across physical, emotional, mental and spiritual domains was used to analyse findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifteen articles met the eligibility criteria for review. Indigenous elder’s spoke to several significant features of Home in ARC settings related to Cultural Home, Physical Home, Emotional/Psychological Home and Relational/Social Home.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Indigenous peoples have differential access to ARC settings as well as unique desires, attitudes and aspirations for thriving in ARC settings. They further bring embodied and rich knowledges into their environments as eminent holders of intergenerational knowledges and cultural practices. Research has demonstrated that homelike environments are favourable in ARC settings. This review advocates for aged care systems to embed culturally relevant care and home practices that prioritise relationality and Indigenous knowledge at the core of service design and delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Indigenous conceptualisations of Home in aged residential care settings: a scoping review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Person-centered care (PCC) has shaped dementia care reforms and informed innovative long-term care models such as care villages. Recreational activities are often seen as a site where PCC is enacted, yet little empirical work has examined how participation in structured activities is enabled, mediated, and constrained through everyday social, relational, and organizational dynamics. This study examines how participation in structured group activities was produced in a care village.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An ethnographic study was conducted in Canada’s first publicly funded care village, drawing on 100 hours of participant observation, 12 staff interviews, and informal resident conversations. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participation varied across activity types and residents’ fluctuating comfort, stamina, and readiness. For many residents, participation was not simply an individual decision, but was scaffolded through staff invitation, accessible information, relational familiarity, and individualized encouragement. It also depended on logistical and organizational conditions, including preparation, transportation, staffing coordination, and role boundaries. These findings show that participation was relationally and organizationally produced rather than simply a matter of resident preference or program design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Structured activities can support meaningful engagement when sustained by relational, logistical, and organizational work. The findings clarify how PCC commitments such as choice, autonomy, and inclusion are enacted through activity systems, while highlighting the labor-intensive conditions required for more equitable participation. These insights have implications for staffing, coordination, and activity provision in care villages and long-term care settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Beyond Attendance: Participation and Relational Work in Planned Group Recreational Activities in a Long-Term Care Village Setting

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS-HCAP) (N = 3,025) in the United States and the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (Mex-Cog) (N = 1071) in Mexico, we examined informant reports of cognitive decline with 17 questions from the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSI-D). Ordinary least squares regression was used to analyze the gender of respondents and informants in each country for the total CSI-D score and logistic regressions for each individual CSI-D question, controlling for correlates of direct and informant measures of cognition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There was no significant relationship between respondents’ gender and total CSI-D reports in either country. Female informants in the United States reported 0.57 more CSI-D symptoms compared to male informants while in Mexico they reported 1.35 fewer symptoms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results show that informant gender is associated with systematically different reporting patterns depending on the national and cultural context in which the assessment takes place. The results suggest that informant reports of cognitive decline may represent social norms in addition to actual cognitive decline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The role of gender in informant reports of cognitive decline in the United States and Mexico

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines differences in the composition and size of the close social network among older adults in same-sex and different-sex coresidential unions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using pooled, probability-based, cross-sectional data from the 2006–2022 Health and Retirement Study, weighted fractional probit and negative binomial regression models were estimated to examine differences in close network composition (proportions of close children, immediate family members, and friends) and network size (number of close ties).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with older adults in different-sex unions, those in same-sex unions reported a higher proportion of friends and a lower proportion of children and immediate family members in their close network, though overall network size was comparable. Supplemental analyses suggested heterogeneity in these patterns. The same-sex versus different-sex gap in friend composition was larger among males than females and was similarly larger among those who were cohabiting than married. Finally, in terms of network size, males in same-sex couples reported smaller close networks than males in different-sex couples, whereas network size was equivalent between females in same-sex and different-sex couples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Beyond their partners, older adults in same-sex unions cultivate distinctly friend-centered close networks. This pattern reflects a history of intentionally built chosen ties that queers dominant assumptions about who partnered older adults designate as close. These findings affirm the importance of policies and practices that acknowledge diverse family arrangements, particularly those rooted in chosen kinship, as a fundamental step toward achieving social equity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Composition and size of close social networks among older adults in same-sex and different-sex couples

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational engagement—here referring to time spent with younger family members—can promote health and happiness. Across adulthood, and particularly in later life, intergenerational engagement represents a potentially meaningful form of social involvement. Using intensive longitudinal methods, we investigated how intergenerational engagement is associated with daily emotional experience and physical activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, 265 participants aged 23–92 completed a 9-day daily diary protocol assessing their intergenerational engagement and emotional experiences; objective physical activity during this period was assessed via tracking steps taken and sedentary minutes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multilevel models revealed significant within-person associations between intergenerational engagement and both emotional experience and physical activity. On days older adult participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater high-arousal positive emotion (happiness, enthusiasm, excitement) during the day. Across the age span of the sample, on days participants spent more time with younger family members, they reported greater low-arousal positive emotion (contentment, relaxation, calm) before bed. Finally, both objective metrics revealed greater physical activity on days with greater intergenerational engagement, whereas other social engagement was unassociated with steps taken or sedentary minutes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings highlight intergenerational engagement as a meaningful daily-life context for both positive emotional experiences and physical activity. For older adults in particular, intergenerational engagement may represent a naturally occurring pathway through which emotionally meaningful social ties support both emotional well-being and opportunities for everyday movement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: More positive and more active: Effects of daily intergenerational engagement on emotion and physical activity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated how grandchild care intensity and community environment influenced frailty trajectories among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, examining whether effects vary by initial frailty status and are moderated by community environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2013, 2015, 2018) combined with 2011 community data, this study included 13,531 respondents (40,593 observations) across 442 communities. Marginal structural models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting were employed to mitigate selection bias. Weighted regressions with community-clustered robust standard errors were constructed, with subgroup analyses stratified by baseline frailty status (non-frail, pre-frail, frail).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While grandchild care showed a null overall effect in the general population, specific impacts varied significantly by baseline frailty status. Intensive caregiving significantly decelerated frailty progression for non-frail adults, whereas moderate caregiving accelerated longitudinal decline among frail adults. Caregiving showed non-significant impacts on frailty trajectory among pre-frail adults. A supportive community environment exerted protective main effects across all subgroups, with the frail group being most affected. It also magnified the protective effects of intensive caregiving on baseline frailty for the non-frail group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a person–environment fit perspective, this study reveals that the health impacts of grandchild care depend on the fit between individuals’ pre-existing health status and caregiving demands, and the role of community becomes more salient as competence declines. Findings highlight the critical need to prioritize vulnerable frail caregivers in health interventions and underscore community development as a key strategy for facilitating healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Competent to care? Grandchild care and frailty trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults through a person-environment fit lens

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender. We examine how gender and Social Security eligibility/receipt are associated with retirement identities, and how these identities are associated with the timing of final workforce exit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Bridge jobs and retirement identities: Gendered life course approach to workforce exits among Early Boomers

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. Yet few studies have examined the role of personal social networks in shaping these geographic disparities. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Personal networks and cognitive health across rural-urban contexts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Positive social connections are key ingredients for healthy aging. We studied older adults’ shared agreement on loving experiences and individual differences in their decisions-making to unlock critical information about how this developmental group connects socially.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To explore shared agreement on experiences of love, we surveyed a representative sample (N=400) of adults aged 65 years and older in the United States. They evaluated 61 experiences to determine whether older adults believe they typically evoke feelings of love in most people. We used a Bayesian decision tree model to account for individual differences in respondents’ knowledge and decision-making styles when deriving the consensus on these experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found a consensus among older adults on experiences of love. In addition, individual differences in knowledge on love and decision-making styles were meaningfully linked to person-level characteristics: female participants and those with higher levels of compassion had higher levels of knowledge on the consensus, White male participants and those with higher levels of loneliness were more likely to guess the shared agreement when they were uncertain, and non-White participants were more likely to guess “True.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Experiences of love for older adults include both romantic and non-romantic settings. Older adults tended to have different knowledge levels regarding the consensus on these experiences. Future research could examine whether fostering compassion or raising awareness about these loving experiences in daily life might improve well-being for older adults. Increased knowledge regarding these experiences may decrease misunderstandings or loneliness by sharing more loving experiences with others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Older Adults share an agreement on experiences that elicit love: A study of consensus and individual differences in judgments

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how exposure to cumulative socioeconomic status (SES) risk in midlife shapes subsequent biological aging among Black American women and tests whether a sense of mastery moderates these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using longitudinal data from 334 middle-aged Black American women in the Family and Community Health Study (FACHS), we used hierarchical regression models to test our hypotheses and probed the interaction by estimating conditional differences between high and low mastery across levels of cumulative SES risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cumulative SES risk was significantly associated with accelerated aging. After accounting for key environmental, psychosocial, behavioral, and biological confounders, each additional risk factor was associated with an increase in GrimAgeAccel of approximately 0.53 years (6.4 months). Among women with lower mastery, cumulative SES risk was positively and significantly associated with accelerated biological aging, with each additional SES risk factor associated with an increase of approximately 0.59 years (7.1 months) in GrimAge acceleration. Cumulative SES risk was not associated with accelerated aging among women with higher mastery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Consistent with stress process theory, higher mastery was associated with a weaker association between cumulative socioeconomic disadvantage and accelerated aging among middle-aged Black American women. Persistent SES-related disparities in biological aging indicate that upstream sociostructural determinants impose a chronic physiological burden that cannot be addressed by individual coping resources alone. Simultaneously bolstering psychosocial resources and addressing the structural conditions that necessitate such high levels of individual coping may be critical for promoting sustained, population-level improvements in healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mastery moderates the association between cumulative socioeconomic status risk and accelerated biological aging among middle-aged Black American women

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others’ intentions during fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning (EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant mini-UG decisions estimated individuals’ tendencies to consider intention vs. outcome information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) decisions across age groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend prior work on age differences in intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural indices

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rural residents are believed to experience greater social isolation than their urban counterparts. This isolation is typically attributed to the structural conditions that distinguish rural communities from urban communities. In the present study, we direct attention to the everyday places that older adults visit across the rural-urban context and the implications this has for direct and indirect social exposure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We leverage ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study. Two hundred and forty-eight participants recorded 4,906 valid EMAs. We explore the probability of EMAs being recorded outside the home and how far each EMA was recorded from home based on driving distance and time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There were no rural-urban differences in the probability of participants being away from home during their EMAs. However, rural participants were located farther from home than urban participants during their non-home EMAs. These latter differences were largely explained by trips to restaurants, stores, and healthcare facilities. There were no observed differences in the time separating participants from their workplaces, other people’s homes, religious centers, or other outdoor spaces.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although rural and urban older adults visit the same types of places at remarkably similar rates, rural residents face greater travel burdens when accessing commercial places (e.g., restaurants, stores, and healthcare facilities). These findings suggest that the rural disadvantage is concentrated in commercial activity and carries implications for the types of social exposures that residents are likely to encounter depending on where they live.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Far From Home? Accessing Everyday Places in Rural and Urban Communities

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study was designed to examine cognitive health disparities in later life. It gathers data on access to social resources, engagement in cognitively stimulating interactions, and exposure to activity spaces.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We enrolled 510 participants from 41 Indiana counties during baseline data collection in Fall 2023. All participants completed a computer-assisted personal interview survey that collected data on their cognitive, mental, and physical health, personal networks, sociodemographic attributes, occupational history, lifestyle activities, and social support. Two hundred and seventy-three participants completed a follow-up module in which they used a smartphone to record ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) that were administered four times per day for seven days.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The mean age was 69.9 years. Most participants were women (64.5%), White (90.2%), and retired (54.5%). The average participant named 5.38 network members. Participants were at home (70.7%) and alone (60.2%) for the majority of their EMAs. Approximately one third of the sample scored below a recommended cutoff for mild cognitive impairment on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conclude by outlining a research agenda that (1) characterizes the social networks, interactions, and place-based activities of participants across geographic contexts, and (2) assesses the potential pathways between a combination of networks, interactions, and activities and cognitive function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Rationale and study design for the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas Study
